title: Same question, but different.
author: D. Cox
summary: D. Cox demonstrates how nine differently-worded questions about the same piece of content -- the Hindu Trimurti -- vary sharply in difficulty despite testing identical knowledge, and argues teachers should deliberately manipulate question wording as a differentiation tool. She lists five factors that inform which version of a retrieval question she chooses for a given student: curriculum position, what she knows about the student, elapsed time since the content was taught, upcoming lesson content, and which parts of the topic are most likely to be forgotten. Working through the nine Trimurti variants, Cox invites the reader to rank them by difficulty and explains what each variation removes or adds -- a letter hint, the number of blanks, whether the answer is named or must be recalled unprompted -- and why that changes the cognitive demand. She connects this practice to three benefits: hitting the "Goldilocks" difficulty zone for a given student, building motivation through appropriately pitched challenge, and preparing students for the variety of question formats they'll meet in formal assessment. Cox closes by mapping the technique explicitly onto several of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, including reviewing prior learning, checking understanding of all students, and obtaining a high success rate.
points: Cox's nine Trimurti question variants test identical content but differ sharply in difficulty depending on whether letter hints are given, how many blanks appear, and whether the answer must be recalled unprompted.

She selects question difficulty based on five factors: curriculum position, knowledge of the individual student, time elapsed since teaching, the content of the upcoming lesson, and likely areas of forgetting.

The technique serves three purposes at once: pitching questions at the "Goldilocks" difficulty level, building motivation through appropriately scaffolded challenge, and preparing students for varied assessment question formats.

Cox explicitly ties the practice to several of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, including reviewing prior learning, checking the understanding of all students, and obtaining a high success rate.
quotes: One way that I differentiate is to consider challenge in the retrieval questions that I ask students.
Forgetting – which content might they be forgetting? Interleaving content from across the topic/course helps to remember in the long term
The Goldilocks effect – not too easy, not too difficult. The middle way. This changes as students learn more and confidence develops.
Making them feel clever can be the biggest motivator. Giving them hints can help. Giving them trickier questions can help students engagement.
So, when you’re asking students questions think carefully; how should I ask this? It makes a difference.
